opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question we got a lot. The short version is that we wanted to know whether recurrence in depth is something a model can actually learn to use as a core capability, rather than something bolted on afterward. If you take an existing pretrained transformer and try to retrofit it with a recurrent block, you're fighting against everything it already learned. Its representations were shaped for a fixed number of layers, a single pass through the network. So when you see a result, it's hard to tell whether you're measuring the idea or just how well you managed the surgery.

Training from scratch gave us a much cleaner experiment. The model learns from the start that it has this recurrent core it can iterate a variable number of times, and during training we sample the number of iterations randomly. So it has to learn representations that stay stable and keep improving as you add compute at test time. We were hoping for that property, that you can just spin the core more often on harder problems and get better answers, and it's something you really want baked in from the beginning.

There was also a scientific motivation. A lot of the current reasoning work happens in token space, with chain-of-thought, where the model verbalizes its intermediate steps. We wanted to ask whether a model can do some of that reasoning in its continuous latent space, without having to write everything out as words. To test that honestly, you need a model whose whole training was built around that mechanism.

Of course, it's expensive. We trained on the order of 800 billion tokens on a pretty substantial chunk of compute, and it was a real engineering effort to get stable training at that scale with a recurrent architecture. We had a few failed runs early on where the model just didn't learn to use the recurrence at all, so the hidden states collapsed. But that was also part of the lesson: the details of initialization, normalization, and how you inject the input at each step matter a lot. In the end, from scratch was the only way to get an answer we'd actually trust.

r001.rationale: The response describes retrofitting an existing pretrained transformer with a recurrent block, then contrasts that with training from scratch to test latent reasoning.

r002.rationale: It says the goal was to iterate the recurrent core more often on harder problems and get better answers.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the short answer is that we didn't really have a choice if we wanted to answer the question honestly. The whole premise of the project is that you can scale test-time compute by recurring in latent space, instead of by producing more tokens. And if you take an existing pretrained model and just try to bolt a recurrent block onto it, you're fighting the model. It was trained to do one forward pass per token. All of its internal representations are calibrated for that depth. So if you suddenly tell it, hey, run this block thirty times now, you mostly get instability and you have to do a lot of fine-tuning just to get back to where you started. And then you can't really tell whether the recurrence is doing anything or whether you've just spent a lot of compute recovering the base model.

Training from scratch lets us bake the recurrence in from day one. The model never sees a world where there is a fixed depth. During training we sample the number of recurrent iterations randomly, and so the model learns to make progress in a way that is robust to being stopped early or run for a long time. That's what gives you the nice property at inference, where you can decide per problem how much compute to spend, and the model actually uses it.

The other reason is more about the science. If we start from a Llama checkpoint, every result is confounded by whatever that model already knew. I wanted to be able to say, this architecture, with this data, trained with this budget, does this. And compare it fairly against a standard transformer with the same budget. That comparison is only clean if both are trained from scratch.

And honestly, part of it was that we had the compute available through the Frontier system at Oak Ridge, and that's a rare opportunity for an academic group. So it felt like the right moment to actually test the idea at a scale where you'd learn something, rather than at a toy scale where everything looks promising and nothing transfers.

r001.rationale: The response says adding a recurrent block to an existing pretrained model would mean bolting recurrence onto a model trained for one forward pass per token, identifying retrofitting a fixed-depth model as an alternative.

r002.rationale: It says recurrence can scale test-time compute and let users choose compute per problem, but does not clearly state that harder problems should receive more computation as a goal of training from scratch.

astra-6.text:
We wanted to study what happens when you build recurrence into the model from the beginning. The idea is that the model can spend more computation on a token by repeatedly updating an internal latent state, rather than having to produce more tokens to think longer.

If you start with a pretrained transformer and add that recurrence afterward, it’s difficult to separate the limitations of the architecture from the difficulty of adapting a model that learned to work differently. Training from scratch gives us a cleaner experiment: can the model learn to use those recurrent steps, and can it benefit from additional steps at inference time?

The tradeoff is that we can’t match the scale of the largest pretrained models. But for understanding whether this approach works, having control over the training process was valuable.

r001.rationale: It describes starting with a pretrained transformer and adding recurrence afterward, identifying retrofitting as an alternative.

r002.rationale: It says recurrence can provide more computation per token and allow additional inference steps, but does not connect that extra computation to harder problems.

sol-6.1.text:
We wanted to study what happens when you give a model more computation in latent space, and training from scratch gave us a clean way to do that. Instead of producing more tokens, the model repeatedly updates an internal representation before it produces an answer.

If you start with a pretrained transformer, its weights have already adapted to a particular architecture and a fixed amount of computation. You can try to turn that into a recurrent model, but then it’s hard to separate the effects of recurrence from the effects of that conversion. We wanted the model to learn from the beginning that it could reuse the same block and refine its representations over multiple steps.

The tradeoff is that we couldn’t start with all the capabilities of a large pretrained model. But for the research question—can a model learn to use additional latent computation, and benefit from more of it at inference time—that was a useful starting point.

r001.rationale: It describes starting from a pretrained transformer and converting it into a recurrent model, identifying that as an alternative to training from scratch.

r002.rationale: It says the goal was to study giving models more latent computation and benefiting from more computation at inference, but does not connect that goal to solving harder problems.
